analysis.one_liner: Requires warrants before the government searches Americans' communications and bans buying personal data from brokers.
analysis.headline: The surveillance reform bill was referred to the House Judiciary and Intelligence committees in March 2026 and no further action has been taken.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would overhaul government surveillance. It would stop federal agencies from searching the communications of Americans collected under Section 702 of the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act without a warrant, ban buying Americans' personal data from data brokers, require warrants for location, browsing, and car data, and add court oversight and accuracy requirements for surveillance applications. It would also extend Section 702 — the program that lets the government collect foreigners' communications — for four years. It has been referred to two House committees and has not moved since.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary Americans whose emails, location data, web history, and car data could otherwise be searched, queried, or bought by federal agencies without a judge's approval. The bill would require a warrant for most government access to that information, ban law enforcement from buying personal data from brokers, and let people challenge surveillance in court. Telecommunications and technology providers also gain limits on what the government can compel them to do.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Ordinary people whose data is searched

how_it_helps.text: Section 101 bars federal officials from accessing Americans' communications gathered under FISA Section 702 without a warrant, consent, an emergency, or a defensive cybersecurity purpose, and requires a written record of every query.

Section 102 stops information collected under Section 702 about people in the United States from being used against them in criminal, civil, or administrative proceedings without the required authorization.
Section 103 bans 'reverse targeting' — spying on foreigners mainly to sweep up the communications of specific Americans — with narrow emergency exceptions.

Title II bars federal law enforcement from buying Americans' personal data from data brokers, including location information and biometric data, and blocks evidence gathered in violation from use in court.

Title VI requires warrants for location, browsing, and search records, and the Email Privacy Act provision requires a warrant for stored emails; Title VII protects car data from federal warrantless searches.

Titles III, IV, and V extend warrant and court-supervision requirements to surveillance conducted outside FISA, add accuracy certifications for surveillance applications, strengthen civil-liberties advocates inside the surveillance court, and add Inspector General oversight.

analysis.who_pays: The intelligence community and federal law enforcement agencies, which would lose warrantless access to Americans' communications and data-broker purchases, and would face new accuracy, court-supervision, and audit requirements. Data brokers would lose a law-enforcement market for location and biometric data.

drawbacks.text: The warrant requirement and query limits include exceptions for emergencies, consent, and defensive cybersecurity, and agencies document their own compliance, which supporters of stronger restrictions say leaves too much to agency self-policing.

By extending Section 702 through 2030, the bill locks in a broad surveillance authority for years in exchange for the new limits; national-security officials and some members of Congress argue the warrant and assistance requirements would slow counterintelligence work and burden telecommunications providers (Sec. 105 makes providers' technical assistance conditional on court approval).

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits are substantial and real: warrant requirements for Americans' data, court oversight of surveillance demands, and a ban on buying location and biometric data from brokers. The costs are genuine but limited by design — exceptions for emergencies, consent, and defensive cybersecurity keep the rules workable, and the security agencies lose convenience rather than core foreign-intelligence capability, since Section 702 itself is extended. The main design risk is enforcement: much depends on audits, attestations, and Inspector General oversight that the agencies being watched must carry out.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the House Judiciary and Intelligence committees on the same day, and neither committee has taken it up since.

narrative.text: H.R. 7901 was introduced in the House on March 12, 2026.

It was referred to both the House Judiciary Committee and the Permanent Select Committee on Intelligence, with a period of consideration 'to be subsequently determined by the Speaker' — the two committees must both act before the House can consider it.
No hearings, markups, or floor votes have occurred; the bill has no action beyond introduction and referral.
The bill would also extend Section 702 surveillance authority to April 20, 2030, making reform the vehicle for reauthorization.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The intelligence agencies and any administration that prefers broad surveillance authority: the current powers remain in place while the bill sits in committee.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Surveillance agencies and the status quo

for.name: Reps. Zoe Lofgren, Pramila Jayapal, and Sara Jacobs
for.what_they_did: Joined the introduction as original cosponsors, giving the bill bipartisan sponsorship.

for.name: House Judiciary and Intelligence Committees
for.what_they_did: Hold the bill; neither has scheduled a markup or moved it since referral.

sides.party_line_note: The bill pairs a Freedom Caucus Republican sponsor with progressive Democratic cosponsors (4 of 217 House Democrats plus 1 other House Republican), a cross-party coalition typical of privacy legislation.

industries.note: FBI, NSA, and other agencies lose warrantless access to Americans' communications and the ability to buy broker data, and face court supervision and Inspector General audits. The bill trades these constraints for a four-year extension of Section 702.

The bill cuts off a federal-law-enforcement market for brokered personal data and subjects broker-sourced data to minimization and transparency reporting. State and local agencies must publicly report purchases made with federal grant funds.

Providers gain a shield: they need not comply with government technical-assistance demands unless a court approves them as necessary and narrowly tailored (Sec. 105). Section 702 itself — and the providers' role in it — is extended four years.

analysis.trajectory: The bill has been referred to two committees — House Judiciary and Intelligence — and neither has taken it up. With five cosponsors and no committee action since March 2026, the most likely path is that it sits until the Congress ends, unless the approaching 2030 Section 702 expiration or an upcoming FISA reauthorization fight gives it a vehicle. Previous similar surveillance-reform packages (including the 2023 version of this bill) also died in committee.
